title: Plans: backlogs, story maps, release maps and estimating
blurb: Choose the right planning artifact, forecast empirically and pick the mapping or estimating technique a scenario calls for.
question: Larkspur Rail's app team has delivered between 18 and 34 story points per sprint. The project manager must forecast when Release 2 will be ready. What should the forecast be based on, and which plan shows it?

teach.h: Plan just enough, just in time
teach.body: The plans practice still defines what will be delivered, by whom, how, when and for how much, so the business case can be met. PRINCE2 Agile changes the form, not the purpose. The release map is the project and stage plan, kept at a high level and updated at stage boundaries. The team plan holds task-level detail for the next iteration only, and is made in managing product delivery. Forecasts come from what the team actually achieves.

teach.body: Most agile methods are empirical: decisions rest on what is happening or has happened. The team starts work, measures how much gets done and forecasts an end date from that rate. Measuring the early rate is called calibration (like zeroing a set of scales) or calculating velocity. The opposite is rationalism, which predicts by reasoning before work starts. A forecast should use the team's own velocity, not another team's or one person's.

teach.caption: Six sprints averaging 26 points. With 260 points of work left, the forecast is about 10 more sprints, if conditions stay the same.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Larkspur Rail's Fair Fares app
teach.body: In initiation, project manager Rhys Pengelly and Matteo Ricci, the chief product owner, build a story map from passenger personas, then cluster the stories into three releases on a release map that references the £3.2 million budget and zero time and cost tolerance. The project backlog holds epics such as 'detect delays'. Rhys forecasts Release 2 from the app team's own average velocity, and leaves task planning to the app team when it accepts each set of user stories from Sasha Ellery, its product owner.

teach.text: Traps: the project backlog (epics, project DoR and DoD) replaces the project product description, while the product backlog (user stories, team DoD) replaces product descriptions. Task-level detail belongs in the team plan for the next iteration, not in the release map. Forecast with the team's own measured velocity, not another team's rate or one person's guess.

items: Release map = project and stage plan: releases of two to four iterations, high level.
Team plan = task level for the next iteration, made by the team on accepting a work package.
Work package description = a set of user stories agreed by the PM and the product owner.
Story map replaces the product breakdown structure; the product flow diagram shows sequence.
Empiricism: start, measure velocity, forecast. Estimates are relative and team-based.

summary: You can now place plans information in the right agile artifact, from release map to team plan and from project backlog to product backlog. You can also forecast empirically from a team's own velocity and choose story mapping, flow diagrams or the right estimating technique for a scenario.

A.q: Callowmere University's Student Support Hub project is in its first delivery stage. Rebecca Lyle, product owner for the web team, has written detailed user stories for appointment booking, each with acceptance criteria, and has linked them to the team's Definition of Done. Where should these stories be held?
options: The project backlog
The product backlog
The release map
The team plan
A.why: The product backlog holds the team's user stories and includes or links to the team Definition of Done; the product owner uses it at team level (8.3.2.1).

whyNot.0: The project backlog holds high-level epics and links the project DoR and DoD; it replaces the project product description, not the team's detailed stories.
whyNot.2: The release map shows how many releases there are, when, and which features each contains; it is not where detailed stories are held.
whyNot.3: The team plan is the task-level plan for the next iteration, produced when the team accepts a work package.

A.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's software team has just finished the first two sprints of Release 1 of the Smart Maintenance project. The board wants a forecast of when the dashboard features in the release will be finished. Which basis for the forecast is MOST appropriate?
options: The team's own velocity measured over these sprints
Senticore's fitting rate on its other customer sites
A task estimate for every story made at initiation
The software team lead's personal estimate of each story
A.why: Agile planning is empirical: start the work, measure how much gets done (calibration or calculating velocity) and forecast from the team's own rate (8.3).

whyNot.1: Another organization's rate for different work says nothing about this team's progress; velocity must be the team's own.
whyNot.2: Detailed task estimates for every story up front is rationalism, planning far too early; task detail is for the next iteration.
whyNot.3: One person's estimate is not the team's measured rate, and agile estimates draw on the whole team.

A.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's Repairs Reimagined project is in initiation. The service design team starts from tenant personas, brainstorms what tenants do when they report a repair, arranges those activities as a journey from first report to job completion, and breaks each activity into user stories. Which planning technique is the team using?
options: A product breakdown structure
A product flow diagram
A user story map
A cumulative flow diagram
A.why: A story map starts from personas, brainstorms user activities, orders them chronologically and breaks them into stories; it is recommended in place of the product breakdown structure (8.3.1, 8.3.2.4).

whyNot.0: A product breakdown structure is a hierarchy of products; PRINCE2 Agile recommends replacing it with the story map described here.
whyNot.1: A product flow diagram shows the sequence and dependencies of products, not user activities arranged as a journey.
whyNot.3: A cumulative flow diagram is a progress technique showing work in each workflow state over time.

B.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's click and collect project is in initiation. Tallis must deliver its stock interface before live stock levels can appear on the website, and live stock levels must exist before customers can reserve and pay. The project manager wants one diagram showing the order in which these products must be created. Which technique should be used?
options: A product breakdown structure
A cumulative flow diagram
A risk-adjusted product backlog
A product flow diagram
B.why: The product flow diagram shows the sequence in which products are developed and the dependencies between them (8.4.2).

whyNot.0: A product breakdown structure shows how products break down into parts, not the order in which they are made.
whyNot.1: A cumulative flow diagram shows tasks in each workflow state over time, to spot bottlenecks.
whyNot.2: A risk-adjusted product backlog holds stories and risk responses together; it does not map product dependencies.

B.q: Larkspur Rail's Fair Fares project is in initiation. About 120 epics and user stories need rough sizes in a single session so that the first release map can be drafted. There is no time to discuss each story at length. Which estimating approach suits this BEST?
options: Card estimating, discussing each story in turn
Magic estimation, sizing many stories quickly
Calibration, running two sprints before sizing
Actual-hours estimates supplied by each team
B.why: Magic estimation is a quick, collaborative technique for early planning, such as at project product level, that sizes many stories without lengthy discussion (8.4.3).

whyNot.0: Card estimating works story by story and suits team estimating; it is slower than magic estimation for sizing a large set at once.
whyNot.2: Calibration measures the delivery rate once work starts; it does not size 120 stories in one session.
whyNot.3: Agile estimating uses relative, not actual, estimates and draws on the whole team together.

B.q: Callowmere University's project manager, Jamal Hussain, has agreed a set of user stories for the next sprint with the web team's product owner. The team now needs a detailed plan of the tasks for that sprint. Who should produce it, and when?
options: The project manager, when authorizing the work package
The chief product owner, at the next stage boundary
The delivery team, when it accepts the work package
Project support, when updating the project dashboard
B.why: The team plan is produced by the delivery team when it accepts a work package, and gives task-level detail for the next iteration (8.3.2, Table 13.12).

whyNot.0: The PM agrees the set of user stories with the PO, but the task-level team plan is the delivery team's own plan.
whyNot.1: Stage boundaries update the high-level release map; task planning for an iteration happens in managing product delivery.
whyNot.3: Project support helps with administration and dashboards; it does not plan the team's tasks.

C.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's click and collect project is at the end of stage 2. In managing a stage boundary, project manager Patrick Dunne produces a task-by-task plan for every sprint of stage 3, assigning each task to a named member of both teams. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the next stage plan is approved at the boundary
Yes, because the fixed date needs detail to protect it
No, because the release map stays high level at this point
No, because stage plans are produced by the delivery teams
C.why: At a stage boundary the plan for the next stage is the release map, kept at a high level; teams plan tasks for the next iteration in managing product delivery, just in time (8.3.2.5).

whyNot.0: The board does approve the next stage plan, but that plan is a high-level release map, so this does not justify task-level detail.
whyNot.1: Time is fixed, but it is protected by flexing scope, not by planning every task in advance.
whyNot.3: Delivery teams produce team plans; the stage plan (release map) is prepared by the project manager.

C.q: Larkspur Rail's new data team has not yet completed a sprint. To fill the release map, project manager Rhys Pengelly forecasts the data team's work using the app team's average velocity of 26 points per sprint, because both teams use two-week sprints. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
options: Yes, because velocity forecasts empirically from experience
Yes, because both teams work to the same sprint length
No, because forecasts at initiation should use rationalism
No, because the data team's own rate must be measured
C.why: Empirical forecasting uses the team's own velocity, found by starting work and measuring it; another team's rate does not reflect this team's work (8.3).

whyNot.0: Velocity is empirical, but only meaningful for the team that produced it, so this reason does not support using the app team's figure.
whyNot.1: A shared sprint length does not make two teams' velocities comparable; story points are relative to each team.
whyNot.2: PRINCE2 Agile favours empiricism over rationalism; the problem is using the wrong team's data.

C.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's project is in initiation. Project manager Sally Greaves replaces the project product description with a project backlog of epics such as 'report a repair with photos'. It links to the project Definition of Ready and Definition of Done and names who will accept the project product. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
options: Yes, because it is the agile form of the project product description
Yes, because epics remove the need for team product backlogs
No, because a project backlog should hold detailed user stories
No, because acceptance responsibilities sit in the quality register
C.why: The project backlog is the PRINCE2 Agile tailoring of the project product description: mostly epics, linking the project DoR and DoD and naming who accepts the project product (8.3.2.1).

whyNot.1: Teams still need product backlogs of user stories; epics in the project backlog do not replace them.
whyNot.2: Detailed user stories belong in product backlogs; the project backlog is mostly high-level epics.
whyNot.3: The quality register records quality activities and results; who accepts the project product is stated in the project backlog.

reteach.title: Planning a long walking holiday
reteach.question: You are walking a 300-mile trail in stages. What do you plan in advance, what do you leave until the day before, and how do you know how far you can go each day?

blocks.body: Before setting off you mark the main legs on a map with rough dates: that is the release map. The night before each day's walk you plan the detail: where to eat, which path, what to carry: that is the team plan. After a few days you know your own pace, say 14 miles a day, and use it to forecast the finish: that is velocity. A friend's pace would not tell you much about yours.

head: Holiday
PRINCE2 Agile
rows: Map of legs with rough dates
Team plan for the next iteration
List of everything you want to see

blocks.text: Planning every meal for the whole trail on day one is planning too early: the weather and your legs will change it. Keep the map high level and plan the detail just in time.

explain.body: The release map is the project and stage plan: how many releases, when, and which features, with budget, tolerances and assumptions included or referenced. The team plan is the delivery team's task-level plan for the next iteration.

test.q: Easterholm County Council's Care Online project is in initiation. The board wants one visual plan showing how many releases there will be, roughly when each is due and which features each contains, with the budget and tolerances referenced. Which artifact meets this need?
options: A team plan
A product backlog
A release map
A project canvas
test.why: The release map serves as the project plan (and, with a shorter horizon, the stage plan): releases, timing and features, with budget, tolerances and assumptions included or referenced (Table 8.1).

whyNot.0: A team plan is task-level detail for the next iteration, not a view of all releases.
whyNot.1: A product backlog lists a team's user stories in priority order; it does not schedule releases.
whyNot.3: The project canvas sets out business justification, not the timing of releases.

explain.body: The project backlog replaces the project product description: mostly epics, linking the project DoR and DoD and naming who accepts the project product. Each team's product backlog replaces product descriptions: user stories, including or linking the team DoD.

test.q: At Draycott Precision Engineering, the high-level requirements for the whole Smart Maintenance project are written as epics such as 'predict failures on Factory A machines'. The list links to the project Definition of Done and names the person who will accept the final product. What is this list?
options: A product backlog
A project backlog
A story map
A work package description
test.why: A project backlog holds high-level epics for the whole project, links the project DoR and DoD and names who accepts the project product (8.3.2.1).

whyNot.0: A product backlog holds one team's user stories and links the team DoD.
whyNot.2: A story map arranges user activities and stories as a journey; it is a planning technique, not the acceptance-linked requirements list.
whyNot.3: A work package description is a set of user stories agreed between the PM and a product owner for a piece of work.

explain.body: Velocity is the average number of story points a team completes per iteration. Divide the remaining points by it to forecast how many iterations are left, assuming conditions stay the same. Use the same team's history.

test.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's e-commerce team completed 28, 32 and 30 story points in its last three sprints. The stories left in Release 2 total 180 points, and conditions are expected to stay the same. About how many more sprints should the team forecast?
options: 5 sprints
6 sprints
7 sprints
9 sprints
test.why: Velocity is the average rate: (28 + 32 + 30) / 3 = 30 points per sprint, and 180 / 30 = 6 sprints (8.3, Glossary).

whyNot.0: Five sprints would need about 36 points per sprint, above any recent sprint.
whyNot.2: Seven sprints assumes about 26 points per sprint, below the measured average of 30.
whyNot.3: Nine sprints assumes 20 points per sprint, which does not match the team's measured history.

explain.body: Agile estimating sizes work relative to other work, not in actual hours, and harnesses the whole team so everyone contributes without being swayed by others. Revealing estimates at the same moment, with numbered cards, is one way to do this.

test.q: In Callowmere University's team planning workshop, each member of the web team holds a set of numbered cards. For each story, everyone chooses a card privately and all turn their cards over at the same moment. Why is the technique used in this way?
options: So the product owner can set the final estimate
So estimates are recorded in actual hours worked
So the PM can compare the speed of individuals
So each view is given without being swayed by others
test.why: Simultaneous reveal lets every team member contribute a relative estimate without being influenced by others (8.4.3).

whyNot.0: The estimate is a whole-team view; the product owner does not set it.
whyNot.1: Agile estimates are relative, such as story points, not actual hours.
whyNot.2: Estimating sizes stories for the team; it is not a way to measure individuals.
